explain.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → The ECMO paradox
explain.intro: Step 3’s key contrast: VA ECMO gives the most flow yet does the least for the left ventricle. Not asked directly, but it is the reasoning behind LV venting and behind the ‘ECPELLA’ combination.
why: **More flow: VA ECMO (>5 L/min) vs Impella 2.5–5 L/min.** ECMO can replace the whole cardiac output.

**Impella unloads and cuts stroke work significantly; VA ECMO fails to unload and increases stroke work (MVO2 unchanged or rising).** ECMO’s retrograde flow raises aortic pressure; a weak LV then ejects less, end-diastolic pressure rises, the aortic valve may stop opening, and the LV distends with pulmonary oedema and stasis thrombus. The fixes are venting: IABP, Impella (ECPELLA) or atrial septostomy.
**Arterial elastance increases on peripheral ECMO.** A steeper Ea line on the PV loop is the picture of the higher afterload (CS-40).
**Gas exchange: VA ECMO +++, the only device.** It is the only one built with an oxygenator; TandemHeart can have one added (CS-51).
mimic: ECMO with a distending LV vs recovering LV
Loss of pulsatility, a closed aortic valve and rising wedge pressure mean the LV needs venting; returning pulsatility means it is recovering.
traps: “The device with the highest flow best protects the ischaemic heart”
VA ECMO perfuses the body but raises LV afterload and oxygen demand; Impella offers less flow but unloads.
decode: Patient on peripheral VA ECMO develops pulmonary oedema and a non-opening aortic valve — mechanism? [pattern]
Raised afterload from retrograde flow, LV distension; vent the LV.
explain.punch: VA ECMO delivers the most flow and the only gas exchange, but its retrograde flow raises afterload so the LV works harder, while Impella delivers less flow and genuinely unloads.

steps.q:
**Name the complication of peripheral VA ECMO**
**described by each, and give its mechanism:**
a Well-oxygenated lower body with a hypoxaemic upper body and cerebral circulation
b Rising pulmonary artery pressures with pulmonary oedema and a flat arterial waveform
c Ipsilateral leg ischaemia after femoral arterial cannulation
steps.a:
a **Differential hypoxaemia** - Harlequin or north-south syndrome. Recovering native cardiac function ejects poorly oxygenated blood from the still-failing lungs into the aortic root and upper body, while retrograde ECMO flow supplies the lower body. Monitor saturation on the **right** hand. Treat by improving native oxygenation or converting to VAV.
b **Left ventricular distension**. Retrograde aortic flow raises afterload against a ventricle that cannot eject, so the LV never unloads. Treat by venting - IABP, Impella, or atrial septostomy.
c **Distal limb ischaemia**. Prevented by siting a distal perfusion cannula at the time of cannulation.
All three follow from one fact: peripheral VA ECMO runs blood backwards up the aorta, against the native heart.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ECMO → Complications of peripheral VA ECMO
explain.intro: Step 6 follows from the plumbing: femoral VA ECMO returns blood up the aorta, against the heart. The three real questions test the two complications that arise from it and their fixes.
why: **Differential hypoxaemia (Harlequin, north-south): a recovering heart ejects blood from failing lungs into the aortic root and upper body, while ECMO flow supplies the lower body; monitor the right hand; treat by improving native oxygenation or converting to VAV.** The two streams meet at a ‘mixing zone’ in the aorta; when the LV recovers, it pushes the zone towards the abdomen, and the coronaries, brain and right arm receive the deoxygenated native output. The right subclavian comes off the brachiocephalic trunk, the first branch of the arch, so the right radial is the first site to show the native output’s low saturation; the femoral side reads high. Raising sweep FiO2 does nothing, because the ECMO blood is already fully oxygenated (left foot 99%). VAV adds a return cannula in the internal jugular, so oxygenated blood enters the right heart, passes the failing lungs and is ejected oxygenated by the LV.

**LV distension: retrograde aortic flow raises afterload on a ventricle that cannot eject, so it never unloads; treat by venting (IABP, Impella, atrial septostomy).** A non-ejecting LV still fills: the venous cannula never drains all the return, so some blood crosses the lungs, and bronchial and Thebesian flow and any aortic regurgitation add to it; pressure rises, the aortic valve stops opening (flat arterial trace, loss of pulse pressure), left atrial pressure rises and pulmonary oedema follows, with a risk of thrombus in the stagnant LV. Lowering ECMO flow and adding an inotrope are the first steps; an Impella pulls blood out of the LV directly (ECPELLA, ACLS-85).

**Distal limb ischaemia: prevented by a distal perfusion cannula at cannulation.** The arterial cannula occludes most of the femoral artery, so the leg beyond it depends on collaterals. A cool, pale, pulseless foot needs an antegrade distal perfusion cannula into the superficial femoral artery at once; heparin, elevation or thrombectomy do not address a cannula blocking the vessel.
mimic: Harlequin vs global hypoxaemia
Harlequin: right hand low, foot high; global: both low, a circuit or oxygenator problem.
LV distension vs good LV recovery
Distension: no pulse pressure, closed aortic valve, rising LA and PA pressures; recovery: rising pulse pressure with an opening valve.
traps: “Harlequin: increase ECMO pump flow”
More flow moves the mixing zone a little closer to the aortic root but raises LV afterload and does not oxygenate the native output; VAV is the definitive fix.
“Harlequin: increase sweep FiO2 to 1.0”
The circuit blood is already saturated; the deoxygenated blood comes from the native lungs.
“Harlequin: convert to VV”
The patient still needs circulatory support for cardiogenic shock; VV removes it.
“Cool pulseless leg: raise heparin, elevate, or thrombectomy”
Place an antegrade distal perfusion cannula.
decode: Femoral VA ECMO, right hand SpO2 84%, left foot 99%, TRALI — best intervention? [DocT GT]
Convert to VAV with a return cannula in the internal jugular vein.
Femoral VA ECMO, right radial severe hypoxaemia, femoral gases good — modification? [DocT GT]
Add a venous return cannula (VAV).
Six hours after right femoral arterial cannulation, cold pale pulseless foot — next step? [DocT GT]
Immediate antegrade distal perfusion cannula into the superficial femoral artery.
explain.punch: Peripheral VA ECMO pumps blood backwards up the aorta: the upper body gets whatever the native lungs and heart send, the LV pushes against the circuit, and the cannulated leg loses its inflow. Put a sensor on the right hand, a vent on the LV and a cannula into the distal leg.

steps.q:
**Place IABP, Impella and VA ECMO in ascending**
**order of circulatory support. For each give:**
a Mechanism
b Approximate flow added
c Effect on left ventricular workload
steps.a:
**IABP**
Counterpulsation - inflates in diastole, deflates in systole. Adds roughly **0.5 L/min**. Modestly reduces afterload and improves coronary perfusion, but needs a native rhythm and some native output.
**Impella**
A microaxial pump drawing blood from the left ventricle into the aorta. Adds roughly **2.5 to 5 L/min** by device. **Directly unloads the LV** - the only one of the three for which that is the primary action.
**VA ECMO**
Full cardiopulmonary support. Adds **4 to 6 L/min** or more, and supports gas exchange as well. **Increases** LV afterload and may need a separate vent.
ECMO gives the most flow and the least unloading. That trade-off is exactly why an Impella is sometimes added to ECMO - the ECPELLA configuration.

explain.sub: Cardiology → Mechanical support → IABP, Impella, VA ECMO
explain.intro: Step 6 closes with the ladder of devices. Each adds more flow, but only one empties the LV, which explains why devices are combined. The real question asked which device works without cardiac synchrony, and the key is narrower than the truth.
why: **Mechanism: IABP inflates in diastole and deflates in systole; Impella is a microaxial pump from LV to aorta; VA ECMO is full cardiopulmonary support.** The IABP is triggered from the ECG or arterial trace, so a fast irregular rhythm or no rhythm defeats it; the Impella and ECMO are continuous-flow pumps that run regardless of rhythm, even in VF.

**Flow: IABP about 0.5 L/min; Impella 2.5–5 L/min by device; VA ECMO 4–6 L/min or more.** The IABP only augments native output and needs some (most sources give 0.5–1 L/min); the Impella’s output depends on the model (2.5 about 2.5 L/min, CP about 3.5–4, 5.0/5.5 about 5–5.5); ECMO can provide a full cardiac output and gas exchange.

**LV workload: IABP modestly lowers afterload; Impella directly unloads the LV; VA ECMO increases LV afterload and may need a vent.** The Impella removes blood from the LV, lowering its volume, wall stress and oxygen use; retrograde ECMO flow does the opposite (ACLS-84). Evidence: IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit, and the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline lists routine IABP as no benefit (3); ECLS-SHOCK (420 patients) found no fall in 30-day mortality with early VA ECMO in infarct-related shock (47.8 vs 49.0%) and more bleeding; DanGer Shock (360 STEMI-shock patients) found lower 180-day mortality with Impella CP (45.8 vs 58.5%) at the cost of more bleeding, limb ischaemia and RRT, and microaxial support is now 2a in selected patients.
mimic: IABP vs continuous-flow devices
Only the IABP needs a native rhythm and output; Impella, TandemHeart and VA ECMO do not.
traps: “Only the Impella works despite an irregular rhythm” (keyed answer)
Only the IABP needs synchrony; TandemHeart and VA ECMO are equally rhythm-independent, and ECMO even supports VF. On the exam pick the keyed Impella if offered, as the classic contrast to the IABP.
“VA ECMO unloads the LV because it gives the most flow”
It raises LV afterload; most flow, least unloading.
decode: Refractory shock with rapid AF — device that does not need cardiac synchrony? [DocT GT]
Impella CP as keyed; strictly, TandemHeart and VA ECMO also qualify, only the IABP does not.
Rank IABP, Impella, VA ECMO by flow, and say which unloads the LV [pattern]
IABP < Impella < VA ECMO; Impella unloads, ECMO loads.
explain.punch: Flow rises from IABP to Impella to VA ECMO, but only the Impella empties the LV and only the IABP depends on the rhythm; ECMO’s full flow loads the ventricle, which is why it is sometimes paired with an Impella.
